lead: Four rules say who has right of way when two boats meet. Two facts decide which one applies: the tack each boat is on and whether they overlap. One boat keeps clear; the other may sail her course.

qa.q: Which racing rule applies when two boats meet: rule 10, 11, 12 or 13?
qa.a: Check tacks first, then overlap: opposite tacks, **rule 10** (port keeps clear); same tack overlapped, rule 11 (windward keeps clear); same tack not overlapped, rule 12 (clear astern keeps clear); past head to wind, rule 13 (tacking boat keeps clear).

blocks.p: Part 2 applies between boats sailing in or near the racing area that intend to race, are racing or have been racing: before the start, on every leg, until you have finished and cleared the line. Between them it replaces the collision regulations. Size, speed, class, the leg you are on and who hailed first change nothing, and a windsurfer is a boat.

blocks.p: Rule 12 exists only on the same tack. On opposite tacks rule 10 decides even when one boat is clear astern, so a gybe by the boat ahead can change who keeps clear.

sections.title: Port keeps clear of starboard

qa.q: Rule 10: does port tack keep clear of starboard even when running downwind?
qa.a: Yes: on opposite tacks the **port-tack boat keeps clear**, whether beating, reaching or running. On a run read the tack from the mainsail: boom to starboard means port tack.

blocks.p: On opposite tacks the **port-tack boat keeps clear**, whether the boats are beating, reaching or running. On a run, read the tack from the mainsail: boom to starboard means port tack. A boat luffing head to wind is still on her old tack.

tiles.name: On a run
tiles.note: boom to starboard: port tack keeps clear

blocks.p: The rule says who keeps clear, not how: cross ahead if you safely can, bear away astern of her, or tack. You kept clear if she could hold her course with no need to avoid you; if she had to alter, you broke the rule, contact or not. No hail is needed, and current, waves or a late duck are your problem. Starboard may still alter course, within rule 16.

On a beat rule 18 does not apply between boats on opposite tacks, so at the windward mark rule 10 stands alone. On a reach or a run starboard keeps right of way but may owe an inside port-tack boat mark-room.

sections.title: Windward keeps clear of leeward

qa.q: Rule 11: who keeps clear when two boats on the same tack are overlapped?
qa.a: The **windward boat keeps clear**, however the overlap began and whoever's bow is ahead. The leeward boat may sail her course and luff, limited only by rules 16.1 and 17.

blocks.p: On the same tack and overlapped, the **windward boat keeps clear**, however the overlap began and whoever's bow is ahead. On a run she is the boat on the side opposite the booms.

tiles.name: Barging at the start

blocks.p: You keep clear with the whole boat, with a margin for gusts. If you cannot point higher, slow down, drop astern or tack away cleanly: the leeward boat may sail her course and may luff, limited only by rules 16.1 and 17. Before the start there is no proper course, so she may luff as far as head to wind, giving you room.

At a starting mark surrounded by navigable water there is no mark-room for boats approaching to start, so a windward boat squeezing in has no rights. With three boats abreast the rule applies to each pair; a middle boat forced onto the leeward one by a boat that did not keep clear is exonerated.

sections.title: Clear astern keeps clear of clear ahead

qa.q: Rule 12: on the same tack, does the boat behind keep clear of the boat ahead?
qa.a: Yes: on the same tack and not overlapped, the **boat clear astern keeps clear**. Waves, surfing and a boat ahead that slows down are her problem; slowing down is not a change of course.

refs: RRS 12, RRS definition Clear Astern and Clear Ahead; Overlap
RRS 11, RRS 12, RRS definition Clear Astern and Clear Ahead; Overlap
RRS 12, RRS definition Leeward and Windward

blocks.p: On the same tack and not overlapped, the **boat clear astern keeps clear**. Surfing, waves, current, a boat ahead stalled or fighting her spinnaker: all the astern boat's problem. The boat ahead may slow down, which is not a change of course, and may alter course to defend her wind if she leaves you room (rule 16.1). Taking her wind is allowed.

tiles.name: You pass to windward
tiles.note: you keep clear all the way: rule 12, then 11

tiles.name: You pass to leeward
tiles.note: once overlapped you have right of way

blocks.p: Leeward and windward exist only between overlapped boats: a hail of "leeward boat" from clear astern gives you nothing. Once your bow, or a bowsprit with its sail set, overlaps her to leeward, rule 11 makes you the right-of-way boat, but you must first give her room to keep clear (rule 15) and may be limited by rule 17.

sections.title: No rights from head to wind to close-hauled

qa.q: Rule 13: when do I lose my rights while tacking, and when do I get them back?
qa.a: From passing head to wind until you are on a close-hauled course you **keep clear of other boats** under rule 13, and rules 10 to 12 do not apply. The rule ends with your heading, even with sails still flapping.

refs: RRS 13, RRS 12, RRS definition Keep Clear

blocks.p: After you pass head to wind you **keep clear of other boats until you are on a close-hauled course**. During that time rules 10, 11 and 12 do not apply, and a hail of "Tacking!" gives you nothing.

blocks.p: The rule ends with your heading, not your trim: sails may still be flapping, and a boat stuck in irons is tacking for as long as it takes. If two boats tack at once, the one on the other's port side, or the one astern, keeps clear. A gybe has no such rule: rules 10 to 12 apply throughout it.

Out of the tack you may hold right of way as starboard, leeward or clear ahead, but rule 15 first gives the other boat room to keep clear. In the zone of a mark to be left to port, rule 18.3 limits you further.
